title: AI Chips for the Agent Era Must Span Both Cloud and Edge
excerpt: Agents push inference demand toward large-scale cloud throughput and toward local responsiveness on cars and home devices. What warrants caution is whether capital and supply chains amplify these demand expectations layer by layer, eventually racing ahead of real, paid usage.
body: When I look at AI chips today, I see two demand curves in my head. The first sits in the cloud, where models need greater concurrency, longer context, and stable sustained throughput. The second sits at the edge, where cars, home devices, and other endpoints increasingly require assistants that respond with low latency, work offline, and keep some data local. Both curves will grow in parallel, yet they call for different chips and different unit economics. The cloud cares about how many inference tasks can be completed per hour. The edge cares about whether a single chip can handle real interactions over time within tight power and device-cost budgets. Reducing both to “we need more GPUs” misses the most important shift coming in the next phase. What worries me more is something else. The demand expectations created by agents could be amplified layer by layer, from cloud service providers, GPU lessors, server vendors, memory suppliers, all the way to financing institutions. Each layer expands capacity based on the orders and forecasts of the layer above, ultimately building supply that outpaces real paid usage. Once the bullwhip effect reverses, the bubble could begin to burst in memory, server, and lease pricing first, before reaching chip-asset returns. So my view has two halves. AI chips remain in an inference-demand expansion phase, and both cloud and edge warrant attention. At the same time, industry risk is rising in lockstep. Judging who gets to keep the profits requires looking beyond compute demand and capex, to how much work these investments actually complete and how much revenue they generate. ## Agents turn inference from a single call into continuous work Ordinary Q&A typically needs one request and one segment of output. Agents first plan, then call search, databases, or other software, read the results back, and continue generating the next step. A single task can therefore involve multiple rounds of model calls, producing longer context and more frequent reads and writes to the KV cache. This changes the workload profile of inference systems. Prefill mainly handles input context and tends to be more compute-bound. Decode generates output sequentially and repeatedly reads model weights and caches. The longer the context, the more memory capacity, bandwidth, inter-chip communication, and scheduling latency become constraints. The number of calls required to complete a task also affects the cost the customer ultimately bears. I use a simple engineering account to track this. ```text Cost per million effective tokens = full system cost per hour ÷ effective tokens produced per hour × 1,000,000 ``` Full system cost includes accelerators, HBM, servers, networking, power, liquid cooling, software, hosting, and depreciation. Effective tokens must be calculated within a specific model, context length, concurrency level, latency target, and quality of service. Inputs, outputs, cache hits, and failed retries cannot be lumped together arbitrarily. Tokens are a common yardstick for comparing service output, but they are not necessarily the unit customers actually buy. Customers may pay per task, per session, per user, or per business outcome. For chip vendors, the central question therefore shifts from peak FLOPS to whether the chip lets customers complete a task at a lower cost. This is also why cloud inference demand will keep growing. The more complex the agent, the more calls each user generates. The longer the model, the more important GPU memory, bandwidth, and interconnect become. Cloud providers need systems that can serve continuously and bill predictably; the occasional peak performance of a single card is not enough to meet that requirement. ## Cloud and edge are two different inference economies The cloud suits centralized handling of large models, long context, and tasks requiring multiple tools to collaborate. Models are deployed centrally, compute can be scheduled across customers, and expensive memory, networking, and liquid cooling can be amortized over more requests. The cloud's main questions are utilization, cost per task, latency, and software fit. The edge faces a different set of constraints. Car assistants and home control hubs need fast response, must keep working when networks are weak, and should handle requests involving home state and personal information closer to the device. The device has limited space, battery or thermal headroom, and the chip cannot transplant data-center power budgets directly. It also has to run reliably for years and cannot be replaced every time the model or software updates. This creates a division of labor between edge and cloud. The edge handles wake-up, sensing, simple decisions, and high-frequency control. The cloud handles complex reasoning, long context, and tasks that require larger models. What data passes between the two, when handoff happens, and how to degrade gracefully on failure all affect both experience and cost. Whether edge demand can become a large-scale chip market depends on several practical questions. Do users engage the assistant frequently enough every day? Are device makers willing to pay more for local inference? Does running locally clearly improve latency and privacy? Can the chip support model updates across the product lifecycle? Cars and home devices are scenarios I will watch closely, but for now product demos alone cannot prove that stable chip demand has formed. The differences between these two curves shape investment judgment. The cloud tends to produce purchase orders and large capex first. The edge has to wait for device shipments, user adoption, and chip design cycles to play out. The cloud verifies faster and at greater asset scale. The edge takes longer to materialize, but once it enters high-frequency device scenarios, demand may be more fragmented and closer to real user behavior. ## HBM, servers, and data centers will expand along with expectations Bottlenecks in inference systems surface layer by layer along the path of data movement. HBM provides capacity and bandwidth. Advanced packaging connects compute chips with memory. Servers and racks organize components into deployable systems. Networking determines whether multiple chips can work together. Power and liquid cooling determine whether the system can keep running. Software scheduling determines how much of this investment turns into billable throughput. In its official introduction of Ironwood TPU, Google frames inference, memory access, and inter-chip interconnect as a single system problem, noting that the largest liquid-cooled configuration connects 9,216 chips and draws close to 10 MW. That is Google's product framing and cannot be extrapolated to a universal standard for all clusters. What it does show is that the supply frontier of the data center has already extended beyond the chip itself. In its Q1 2025 earnings call, TSMC said CoWoS demand was fully booked and that it planned to expand capacity. In its June 2025 results materials, Micron linked data-center DRAM revenue growth to HBM demand and capacity-expansion investment. Demand growth and capacity expansion are happening at the same time. Cloud providers design their own accelerators accordingly and lock in server, memory, and data-center capacity ahead of time. The condition for a specialized chip is that the workload is stable enough, that software porting cost is manageable, and that long-term utilization can cover R&D, deployment, and maintenance outlays. AWS's Trainium, Inferentia, and Neuron software stack, and Google's TPU, are examples of building system capability around specific cloud workloads. The issue is that supply chains typically see demand signals earlier than end-user paid behavior. Cloud providers, seeing customer inquiries, raise procurement plans. GPU cloud service providers, seeing long-term lease contracts, build new data centers. Server vendors, seeing orders, add inventory. Memory and packaging vendors, seeing expansion plans, keep investing capex. Financing institutions then treat these contracts and assets as the basis for future cash flow. When the same expectation is reused at multiple stages, the bullwhip effect appears. No single layer needs to wait for the final task to materialize, yet supply has already been pulled forward. As long as agent demand keeps growing, this mechanism helps the industry build capacity quickly. The moment demand growth slows, the inventory, depreciation, and interest costs accumulated upstream will all look for an exit. ## A bubble may start breaking at asset returns I do not treat “memory will be oversupplied tomorrow” as the current conclusion. HBM may still benefit from high-bandwidth inference, and edge devices may bring new storage and compute demand. What I want to observe is whether capital deployment has already moved fast enough to disconnect some segments from real usage. In June 2025, Applied Digital disclosed that it had signed two approximately 15-year lease agreements with CoreWeave, providing 250 MW of IT load. Contracts of this kind support the early build-out of data-center capacity and let financing institutions form a view of future cash flow. In a 2026 discussion on AI infrastructure financing, BIS analyzed how corporate debt, private credit, joint ventures, and off-balance-sheet arrangements jointly support expansion. None of this proves that demand is fake on its own. It converts future revenue into assets that can be built and bought today, and turns operating judgment into financial contracts. What truly needs to be checked is whether contract tenor, debt tenor, GPU economic life, equipment iteration speed, and customer payment cycles are aligned. If customers keep using the service, long-term contracts help amortize build-out costs. If effective-token growth, customer renewal, or GPU utilization falls short of procurement assumptions, lease, depreciation, power, and interest costs still accrue under the contracts. The equipment can keep running while asset returns have already declined. After that, GPU lease prices, residual values of used equipment, server inventory, and some memory prices all come under pressure. This is also why I put both A and C into the risk view. Demand mismatch means too much equipment chasing too little paid call. Supply-chain expansion then propagates that mismatch to HBM, standard DRAM, servers, packaging, and data centers. A bubble does not necessarily start bursting because model demand suddenly vanishes; it can start when some segment finds that incremental orders no longer cover its cost of capital. ## Where the profits land Cloud inference profits will flow first to those who can fold multiple constraints into a single system. GPU designers hold chip performance, software ecosystem, and supply-chain control. Cloud providers hold models, customers, scheduling, and the billing entry point. HBM and advanced-packaging suppliers hold pricing power when supply is tight. Their advantages come from different sources and last for different durations. GPUs will retain versatility for training, model development, and fast-changing inference tasks. Cloud providers' in-house chips suit recurring workloads, but software porting, developer tools, and customer compatibility constrain how far they can expand. HBM and advanced packaging earn premiums more easily when supply is tight; once capacity expands, certification cycles, yield, alternative paths, and customer concentration become more important. On the edge, profits do not necessarily sit only with chip designers. Carmakers, phone makers, and home-device vendors own the product entry point, while chip suppliers must balance power, cost, model tooling, and long-term support. Companies worth watching are those that can embed chips into high-frequency products and have local inference improve user experience or reduce cloud call costs. My investment filter starts with three questions. First, what outcome does the customer pay for. Second, does the supplier improve task cost, latency, power, or supply certainty. Third, once order growth arrives, do utilization, gross margin, and cash returns follow. Leading on a single metric can earn a premium for a while, but the ability to keep delivering tasks is what gives a premium staying power. ## The signals I will wait for On the cloud side, I will watch whether cloud providers disclose effective tokens, utilization, quality of service, and output per megawatt, and whether capex growth translates into cloud service revenue and cash flow. Higher peak throughput alone is not enough to change the judgment. On the supply chain, I will compare moves in HBM, standard DRAM, server, and GPU lease prices, and watch for divergence between inventory and delivery lead times. Whether equipment keeps working stably after deployment and whether customer contracts get renewed matters more than how much capex is announced. On the edge, I will look at actual shipments of cars and home devices, assistant usage frequency, the share of workloads run locally, and product gross margin. Product demos can prove technical feasibility; sustained usage is what proves chip demand exists. If paid tokens lag compute supply over the long term, or if cloud providers' in-house chips remain stuck at internal demos, the industry view needs to come down. If complex agent tasks generate sustained paid calls, edge devices start handling high-frequency, low-latency work, and unit inference cost keeps falling, then dual demand from cloud and edge can truly support the next round of chip investment. ## Key sources - [Groq Inference Tokenomics, Speed, But At What Cost?](https://semianalysis.com/2024/02/21/groq-inference-tokenomics-speed-but), SemiAnalysis, 2024-02-21 - [Mastering LLM Techniques, Inference Optimization](https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/mastering-llm-techniques-inference-optimization), NVIDIA, on Prefill, Decode, and KV Cache - [Ironwood TPU](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/infrastructure-and-cloud/google-cloud/ironwood-tpu-age-of-inference/), Google, 2025-04-09 - [TSMC Q1 2025 Earnings Call Transcript](https://investor.tsmc.com/english/encrypt/files/encrypt_file/reports/2025-04/7630274eecc1197a4e3ea6a415f44a47204fe10a/TSMC%201Q25%20Transcript.pdf), TSMC, 2025-04 - [Micron FY2025 Q3 results](https://investors.micron.com/news-releases/news-release-details/micron-technology-inc-reports-results-third-quarter-fiscal-2025), Micron, 2025-06-25 - [AWS Neuron SDK 2.26.0](https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2025/09/aws-neuron-2-26-announce/), AWS, 2025-09 - [Applied Digital Announces 250MW AI Data Center Lease With CoreWeave](https://ir.applieddigital.com/news-events/press-releases/detail/123/applied-digital-announces-250mw-ai-data-center-lease-with), Applied Digital, 2025-06-02 - [Financing the AI infrastructure boom](https://www.bis.org/publ/qtrpdf/r_qt2603u.htm), BIS, 2026-03-16 - [AI agents for the smart home](https://www.home-assistant.io/blog/2024/06/07/ai-agents-for-the-smart-home), Home Assistant, 2024-06-07
